intro: Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s First Ballade, where a quiet G-minor melody and an E♭-major song return with alarming force. The last word belongs to a coda marked Presto con fuoco — very fast, with fire.

sections.label: Intro · Octaves climbing from the bass
sections.mNote: Both hands climb together, then stop on a dissonance

sections.label: A · G minor, quietly
sections.mNote: A circling melody over detached bass notes and chords

sections.label: B · The E♭-major song
sections.mNote: A broad melody above gently rolling left-hand chords

sections.label: Dev · A minor turns to A major
sections.mNote: The first theme returns; the second answers in full chords

sections.label: B′ · The song in full chords
sections.mNote: The E♭-major melody returns fortissimo over sweeping broken chords

sections.label: A′ · G minor over a low D
sections.mNote: The first theme returns quietly above repeated bass notes

sections.label: Coda · Presto con fuoco
sections.mNote: Leaping chords and displaced accents drive the fast ending

sections.label: C · Scales, chords and silences
sections.mNote: Runs cross the keyboard between heavy G-minor chords

cues.title: An octave apart
cues.text: Both hands start on C and climb an octave apart, outlining A♭ major. The marking is Largo. The line reaches the treble, hesitates, and settles into chords with an E♭ rubbing against D below it.
cues.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 23, Klindworth edition (Bote & Bock, c. 1880), bars 1–7. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1959
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: G minor, quietly
cues.text: The piano settles into Moderato and a broad six-beat bar. A circling G-minor melody sings above detached bass notes and chords. The hands have separated: one speaks, the other keeps the phrase moving.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 8–16: 6/4, Moderato, and the first theme’s detached left-hand accompaniment.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The E♭-major song
cues.text: The second theme opens in E♭ major, marked meno mosso — less movement. Long notes in the right hand float above the left hand’s rolling chords. The phrase has room to spread across several bars.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, pickup in bar 67 and theme in bars 68–81; E♭ major and meno mosso.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A minor over E
cues.text: The first melody returns in A minor. Low repeated Es take the place of the opening accompaniment, and the tune begins quietly again. Its next answer will come from the second theme, in A major.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 94–106: first-theme return over repeated E; A-major second theme at bar 107.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The song finds its voice
cues.text: The second theme arrives in A major with full right-hand chords and a low A in the bass. What began as a gently accompanied song now fills both ends of the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 106–113: E dominant harmony resolves to A major; chordal second theme above left-hand arpeggios.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Chopin’s own favourite
cues.text: In Leipzig in 1836, Schumann tells Chopin that this Ballade is his favourite of Chopin’s works. Chopin thinks for a long time. Then, in Schumann’s account, he replies: “I’m glad of that because it’s the one I prefer too.”
cues.evidence: Schumann’s account of the 1836 Leipzig meeting, quoted by Orrin Howard in the LA Phil programme note. https://www.laphil.com/works/ballade-no-1-in-g-minor-op-23

cues.title: E♭ major, fortissimo
cues.text: The second theme returns first, in its original E♭ major. Chopin marks it fortissimo and sends the left hand sweeping through broken chords. The tune has kept its long notes; the piano beneath them is in full flight.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 166–179: fortissimo return of the second theme, with continuous left-hand broken chords.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The first tune whispers
cues.text: G minor returns with the first theme, marked meno mosso. The left hand repeats a low D very quietly. This recollection is short: D-major chords soon gather underneath it, preparing the coda.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 194–207: quiet first-theme return, repeated D bass and dominant preparation.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Presto con fuoco
cues.text: The coda starts with a low G and leaping chords. Presto con fuoco: the six-beat sway is gone. Accents land inside the bar, and the right hand repeatedly drops from a high chord to a single lower note.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 208–215: Presto con fuoco, change from 6/4 to 4/4, low G and displaced right-hand chord accents.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Scales and silences
cues.text: A low G holds the floor while scales sweep up the keyboard. Heavy G-minor chords interrupt the runs; pauses interrupt the chords. The final descent comes in octaves, step after chromatic step, before the last G.
cues.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 250–264: sustained bass G, ascending scales, interrupted chordal passages and chromatic octaves.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Octaves become a quiet melody
transitions.from: Intro · Octaves climbing from the bass
transitions.how: The Largo ends with E♭ above a bass D. At Moderato, the metre changes to 6/4 and the hands separate into melody and accompaniment. A low D introduces the quiet G-minor theme, followed by detached bass notes and chords.

transitions.title: The runs leave room for E♭
transitions.how: The running figures dwindle and stop. Under meno mosso, a long right-hand phrase opens in E♭ major while the left hand rolls gently through its chords. The six-beat bar remains, but the melody now stretches across it.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 62–75: smorzando, rests, meno mosso and E♭-major second theme.

transitions.title: The first melody moves to A minor
transitions.to: Dev · A minor turns to A major
transitions.how: The E♭-major song slows through its last decorated phrases. Repeated low Es then underpin the first theme in A minor. The accompaniment begins quietly and thickens into E dominant chords, ready for the second theme’s A-major answer.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 90–107: first-theme return in A minor over E, followed by E dominant harmony and A major.

transitions.title: A falling run reaches the song
transitions.from: Dev · A minor turns to A major
transitions.to: B′ · The song in full chords
transitions.how: A long descending run reaches B♭ in the bass. The lyrical theme returns above it in full chords, fortissimo, and the bass moves to E♭. The left hand keeps sweeping through broken chords beneath the melody.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 164–169: descending run, B♭ bass at bar 166, E♭ at bar 167 and chordal second-theme return.

transitions.title: The bass settles on D
transitions.from: B′ · The song in full chords
transitions.to: A′ · G minor over a low D
transitions.how: The right-hand runs slow and fall towards the middle of the piano. At meno mosso, the first theme returns in G minor above repeated low Ds, marked pianissimo. The broad E♭-major song has shrunk to a quiet recollection.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 188–199: rallentando, meno mosso and repeated D bass under the first theme.

transitions.title: D major releases the coda
transitions.from: A′ · G minor over a low D
transitions.how: D-major dominant chords gather beneath the descending right hand. The coda answers with a low G, Presto con fuoco, and a new four-beat bar. High chords leap down to single notes while the left hand alternates bass notes and chords.
transitions.evidence: Klindworth edition, bars 206–211: D dominant harmony, low G and the change from 6/4 to 4/4 at the coda.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
